title: Keep your routine
steps: Keep your normal sleep window
Complete tomorrow's check-in
rationale: Your signals are close to your personal normal.

title: Protect tonight's sleep
steps: Keep the hour before sleep free of screens and work
Keep your sleep station dark and cool
rationale: Your sleep was a little shorter or lighter than usual; a steady sleep window helps your immune system.

title: Take a saliva sample
steps: Collect a saliva sample before breakfast
Run the viral DNA test on the onboard analyser
Repeat the check-in this evening
rationale: Early changes in your temperature, heart rate or breathing can come before a dormant virus wakes up; a saliva test shows whether one is active.

title: Recover your sleep
steps: Ask to keep tonight's sleep window free of tasks
Dim the cabin lights an hour before sleep
Skip caffeine after midday
rationale: Several short or broken nights weaken your immune defences; recovering sleep is the quickest fix.

title: Take time to unwind
steps: Take a 20-minute break away from your workstation
Use your next private call to talk to someone you trust
Tell the commander if your workload feels too high
rationale: Stress can let dormant viruses wake up; small breaks and talking it through help.

title: Rest and watch
steps: Prioritise sleep tonight
Repeat the check-in this evening
rationale: Some signals moved away from your normal; most changes like this settle with rest.

title: Reduce workload: VZV is active
steps: Ask the commander to move non-critical tasks
Check your skin each morning and photograph any change for the medical officer
Repeat the saliva test in 48 hours
rationale: VZV in saliva means the virus behind shingles has woken up; rest and an early medical review help it pass faster.

title: Look after the rash
steps: Keep the rash covered and don't share towels
Photograph the rash each morning for the medical officer
rationale: A rash or tingling patch can spread to crewmates through shared items, and photos show the medical officer how it changes.

title: HSV-1 is active: protect the crew
steps: Don't share cups, cutlery or towels
Repeat the saliva test in 48 hours
rationale: HSV-1 in saliva means cold sores can appear and spread through shared items.

title: Care for mouth sores
steps: Don't share cups, cutlery or towels
Photograph the sores for the medical officer
rationale: Mouth sores spread through shared items, and photos show the medical officer how they change.

title: EBV is active: rest
steps: Avoid heavy exercise until the medical officer clears you
Repeat the saliva test in 48 hours
rationale: EBV in saliva means the virus is active; rest lowers the strain on your body.

title: Rest your throat and glands
steps: Drink water regularly through the day
Check in again tomorrow morning
rationale: A sore throat or swollen glands can mean your body is fighting a virus; fluids and rest help.

title: Limit spread to the crew
steps: Wear a mask in shared modules
Eat apart from the crew until the medical officer says otherwise
Wipe shared handles and controls after use
rationale: Fever or chills can mean an infection that could pass to your crewmates.

title: Check the inflammation result
steps: Repeat the blood test tomorrow morning
Limit time in shared modules until the result is back
rationale: A raised CRP or white cell count means your body is fighting something.

title: Tell the crew medical officer
steps: Share today's status with the crew medical officer
Ask the commander to lighten today's schedule
rationale: Several signals point the same way; a medical review catches problems early.

title: Check your oxygen level
steps: Sit upright and rest
Measure your oxygen saturation again with the medical kit
Call the crew medical officer now if it stays low
rationale: Low oxygen saturation needs a check straight away.

title: Isolate and get medical help
steps: Move to your crew quarters and wear a mask
Contact the crew medical officer now
Send today's data to the flight surgeon
rationale: High risk of an active infection that could spread to the crew.
